--- title: "Housing and racial bias" subtitle: "Names and greetings in emails to public housing authorities, 2014" bibliography: [references.bib, references-new.bib] --- The Housing and racial bias case study examines one claim from a field experiment on how officials of public housing authorities in the United States answer emails from people who wish to apply for housing, published in the *American Journal of Political Science* by the original authors [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. The claim was reanalysed by five independent analysts in the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], while a new experiment conducted for the SCORE replicability study attempted to replicate it. Page numbers in quotations from the paper refer to the accepted manuscript, which is openly available at [OpenBU](https://hdl.handle.net/2144/37826). ## 1. The original study {#sec-study} ### 1.1 Street-level bureaucrats {#sec-question} @Lipsky1980StreetLevelBureaucracy called the officials who deliver public services in direct contact with citizens 'street-level bureaucrats', a term that draws attention to the discretion held by such officials, given that the rules that these officials apply never settle every case and that the way in which an official treats one applicant rather than another can decide who receives a benefit. Public housing in the United States is scarce and is administered by local authorities under federal rules, and since 1998 those authorities have had wide freedom in selecting tenants, with the consequence that "local offices and officials have discretion over policies they did not themselves design" (p. 7). The original authors asked whether racial and ethnic bias, which earlier experiments had found among politicians and election officials, also reaches "bureaucracies that provide access to valuable government programs and are less tied to politics" (abstract), and the authors' first hypothesis, from whose test the claim comes, reads "All else equal, bureaucrats will be less responsive and less friendly to blacks and Hispanics than they are to whites" (p. 5). ### 1.2 Audit studies {#sec-audits} An audit study measures discrimination by sending requests that are identical except for one characteristic of the sender, assigned at random, and by comparing how these requests are answered, the studies of hiring and of public officials that made the design familiar being presented in the module [Audit experiments](companion/experiments.qmd#sec-audits). Given that the characteristic is assigned at random, the groups of requests differ only by chance in every other respect, and a difference in the answers can therefore be read as the effect of that characteristic. What such a design manipulates, however, is a name, and a name conveys to its reader more than one thing about the sender, a point to which section 5 returns. ### 1.3 The design {#sec-design} The original authors emailed "all public housing authorities that could plausibly be matched with a core city in a metropolitan or micropolitan area (n = 1017)", and "Each housing authority received an email on one of two days in the same week during 2014" (p. 8). Each authority was assigned at random to one of six email accounts, comprising a male and a female name meant to indicate each of three groups (@tbl-names). While the white and Black first names were drawn from lists of names distinctive of each group, the Hispanic names rely mainly on the surname Martinez, nearly 92% of whose bearers are Hispanic (p. 9). The authors were able to match the ages suggested by the white and the Black names, but not the ages suggested by the Hispanic names, which "peak in the 1990s and 2000s" (p. 10). ::: {#tbl-names .cell tbl-cap='The six names of the experiment, with the emails sent and delivered, the replies and the share of replies with a greeting code that opened with the name of the sender. Source: `data/display_names.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Name Meant to indicate Sent Delivered Replies Reply rate Greeted by name
Brett White 172 172 96 55.8% 60.4%
Emily White 145 136 81 59.6% 62.0%
Tyrone Black 184 184 116 63.0% 59.1%
Shanice Black 145 142 82 57.7% 51.9%
Santiago Hispanic 207 202 106 52.5% 37.1%
Gabriela Hispanic 161 155 82 52.9% 46.3%
``` ::: ::: Every authority received the same text, in which the sender's name stood in place of X (p. 10): > Hello, > > My name is X and I'm trying to figure out how to apply for public housing. I believe I may be eligible. > > Can you direct me to information about applying for public housing here? I also heard there might be a wait list for this program. How long is it? > > Thanks, X For 45% of the authorities the address was taken from the list maintained by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), a case recorded as a 'Hard Email' (p. 11). The replies were coded for whether the authority replied at all, whether it replied within 24 hours and whether it gave the length of the wait list, as well as for tone, measured by "whether the emailer is addressed by proper name. We were lenient in coding 'yes.' A named salutation could be as causal [sic] as 'Hi Brett' or as formal as 'Dear Ms. Martinez.'" (p. 12). A cold reply can discourage an applicant, and tone, the authors argue, "can affect the ultimate distribution of benefits in subtle but important and under-appreciated ways" (p. 2). ### 1.4 The results {#sec-results} The authorities replied at similar rates to every group, 60.7% to Black names against 57.5% to white names (p. 15), and the gap of 4.8 points between white and Hispanic names is described as "fairly small and borderline significant (with a one-tailed test)" (p. 15), with p = .11, while two-sided the same gap in the public file has p = 0.214. The tone of the replies, however, differed: "Sixty one percent of the messages to the white emailers began with a named salutation. Only 41% to Hispanics did." (p. 18). The third model of Table 1, a logistic regression of the greeting on the three groups of names that also includes percent Black, percent Hispanic, poverty rate and logged population of the community (2012 American Community Survey) and the Hard Email indicator, yields a coefficient of −0.82 for the Hispanic names, with a standard error of 0.22, on 549 replies (p. 37). Expressed as a change in the predicted probability of a named greeting from a white to a Hispanic name, with the other variables held at their means, this coefficient corresponds to −20.0 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from −30.5 to −10.0 (p. 18). A footnote adds that coding every email without a reply as an unfriendly reply "does not affect the results" (p. 18, note 11), and officials with Hispanic names, the paper also reports, greeted Hispanic names by name not significantly more often than other officials did, 47% against 40% (p. 19). ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Share of replies with a greeting code that opened with the name of the sender, by name, with 95% Wilson intervals. Source: `data/display_names.csv`.](background_files/figure-html/fig-names-1.png){#fig-names fig-alt='Dot plot of six names with intervals. Brett, Emily and Tyrone lie near 60%, Shanice near 52%, Gabriela near 46% and Santiago near 37%; the two Hispanic names are drawn in burgundy.' width=672} ::: ::: The abstract states the finding in the sentence from which the claim was taken: "Hispanic housing applicants were twenty percentage points less likely to be greeted by name than were their black and white counterparts" (abstract). The twenty points, however, correspond to the comparison with white names, whereas against the white and Black names together the raw gap among replies is −17.3 points. ## 2. SCORE {#sec-score} ### 2.1 Reproduction, robustness and replication {#sec-repetition} SCORE, short for Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence, subjected claims from published social and behavioural research to three kinds of repetition [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen]. A reproduction repeats the original analysis on the original data, a robustness check applies different but defensible analyses to the same data, and a replication asks the same question of new data. The three studies, the SCORE reproducibility study, the SCORE robustness study and the SCORE replicability study, were reported in *Nature* in 2026 [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial], and the paper examined here went through two of them. Although its data and code are public, the reproduction component for this paper on the Open Science Framework (OSF) holds only an unfilled template, and the record of the robustness study marks the reproduction as never attempted, with every component of the record on the OSF linked from the [Resources page](resources.qmd#the-case). ### 2.2 The claim and the Task 2 instruction {#sec-robustness} The robustness study assigned claims from 100 studies in the SCORE sample to independent analysts, 457 people who carried out 504 reanalyses in all [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136]. Each claim is a sentence, taken from the abstract where possible, that corresponds to one statistically significant test, and where the lead team judged an expression "to be ambiguous or rhetorical, they replaced the expression with an ellipsis mark" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods]. In the case of the housing experiment, the claim reached the analysts in the following form. > "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" (p. 100 of the published article) The ellipses in the claim remove "20 percentage points" ("twenty" in the accepted manuscript) and "their black and". As selected, the claim therefore compares Hispanic names with white names only and states a direction without a size, whereas the abstract compares the Hispanic names with Black and white names together and puts the gap at twenty points, and the five analysts, taken together, tested both versions. In Task 1 of the robustness study, each analyst examined the data in whatever way seemed best to the analyst and drew one of four conclusions: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis. In Task 2, each analyst then produced a single statistical result under instructions that "always remained circumstantial (for example, data selection, exclusions and choice of measurement)" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods], and the instruction given for the housing claim read as follows. > "You should disregard the moving locations' ethnical composition from which/to which applications were sent." Since nobody in the experiment was moving, the instruction can arguably mean only that the ethnic composition of the communities – percent Black and percent Hispanic – should be left out of the model. ## 3. The five reanalyses {#sec-reanalysts} All five analysts worked from the public file deposited by the original authors, on which the course refits each analysis from its script, or in the case of UYV3F from its report, reproducing the four recorded statistics exactly. The choices made by each analyst in Task 2 are presented in @tbl-analysts, under the identifiers assigned to the analysts by the robustness study. ::: column-body-outset ::: {#tbl-analysts .cell tbl-cap='The five reanalyses in Task 2, with the statistic as recorded in the robustness study and the conclusion of Task 1. Source: `data/analysts5.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Analyst Discipline Hours Comparison Emails counted Method Emails analysed Recorded statistic Task 1 conclusion
8PTRZ Computer Science/Statistics/Data Science 2 Hispanic against other names replies chi-square test of independence (continuity-corrected) 558 χ2 = 14.265 evidence for the claim
UYV3F Psychology 9 Hispanic against white names replies logit, no covariates 362 z = −3.771 evidence for the claim
EWFMI Psychology 2.5 Hispanic against white names (three-group model) replies logit with name sex, poverty third (as a number) and hard-to-find email 549 z = 3.645 evidence for the claim
25N5D Sociology 3 Hispanic against white names all delivered emails two-proportion test (continuity-corrected) 665 χ2 = 13.683 no evidence either way
P9W8Y Psychology 25 three groups replies logit, omnibus likelihood-ratio test and Tukey-adjusted pairs 558 none recorded no evidence either way
``` ::: ::: ::: ### 3.1 Five questions {#sec-questions} **UYV3F** compared Hispanic with white names among the replies – the comparison of the claim as selected – in a logistic regression without covariates. Since such a model reproduces the two observed shares, it estimates the raw gap in the paper, −20.0 points, and the analyst's report states the hypotheses as one-sided, "H0: β1 ≥ 0 vs. H1: β1 < 0". **EWFMI** made the same comparison in Stata, in a model of all three groups adjusted for the sex of the name and the Hard Email indicator, with the poverty third of the community entered as a number from 1 to 3. Having dropped, in line with the instruction, the Hispanic third that the Task 1 model had included, the analyst obtained an adjusted gap of −19.4 points. **8PTRZ** made the comparison of the abstract, between Hispanic names and the white and Black names together, using the test of a two-by-two table. `chisq.test()` in R applies a continuity correction to such a table by default, making the test slightly more conservative, and the value recorded in the robustness study is the corrected one. The resulting gap of −17.3 points is smaller than that against white names alone, since Black names were greeted by name less often than white ones. **P9W8Y** fitted a logistic regression on all three groups and reported the test of whether the three differ at all, followed by pairwise comparisons. Such an omnibus test answers a broader question than the claim, given that it would reject equality just as readily if the Black names were the ones greeted less often. Although the analyst's report gives a $\chi^2$ on 2 degrees of freedom, the robustness study recorded no statistic, and the course places the analysis by its gap between Hispanic and white names, −20.0 points. **25N5D**, the one sociologist among the five, began from the comparison made in the paper and then questioned it: "this naive estimate suffers from post-treatment bias. Signaled Hispanic names (the treatment) affect whether the bureaucrat responds; then, we condition only on bureaucrats who respond to investigate whether they use the applicant's proper name." Following @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias, the analyst counted every delivered email, treating an email without a reply as one without a named greeting, a redefinition under which the gap shrinks to −13.2 points but remains significant. ### 3.2 Comparing among replies {#sec-posttreatment} Since the names were assigned to housing authorities at random, the authorities that received each name are alike in expectation, but the same cannot be said of the replies, which were not assigned at random. If the name changes whether an official replies, the officials who answered Santiago need not resemble the officials who answered Brett, and a comparison of greetings among replies then mixes the effect of the name on how officials write with a difference in which officials wrote. Conditioning on a variable that the treatment can change is known as post-treatment conditioning, a practice that can produce a difference between groups even where the treatment has no effect on the outcome [@MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment]. @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias discusses the problem in audit experiments, in which the content of replies is a common outcome, and the redefinition chosen by 25N5D is one of the remedies. The remedy, however, changes the question. Counting every delivered email preserves the groups as randomisation made them, and the gap of −13.2 points is therefore an effect of the name on receiving a reply that opens with the name of the sender. Such an outcome combines whether a reply came with how it began, and since only 53% to 61% of the emails in each group drew a reply, the gap among all emails is smaller almost by construction. The comparison among replies, by contrast, answers the question posed by the claim, about the tone of the replies that came, yet it corresponds to a pure effect of the name only if the name did not change who replied. The gap in replies between white and Hispanic names, −4.8 points (p = 0.214), appears to make a large selection unlikely without ruling it out, and the course retains both comparisons as defensible answers to two related questions. ### 3.3 Two verdicts of no evidence {#sec-verdicts} Three analysts concluded in Task 1 that the data showed evidence for the claim, while the other two ticked "The results do not show evidence for or against", although the work of each of these two analysts shows a significant gap. 25N5D concluded that "Hispanic housing applicants were less likely to be greeted by name than white applicants, though the magnitude of the effect is substantially smaller than that reported in the original results", a verdict that seems to judge the claim by the twenty points of the abstract, which the claim as selected had removed. P9W8Y concluded that "The results do not provide evidence of a relationship between ethnicity and friendliness (proper name) on the received e-mails." The model used in Task 1, however, included the interaction of ethnicity with the sex of the name, and in such a model, with the default coding of R, the test of ethnicity compares the three groups among the female names alone, the female names forming the reference category of sex. Refitted on the public file, the test among the three female names gives p = 0.128, the value reported by the analyst (0.13), whereas in Task 2, without the interaction, the same analyst found that Hispanic names were greeted by name less often than white and Black names. One verdict appears to rest on the size of the effect and the other on a narrower test than the analyst intended, and neither disputes the direction of the gap. ## 4. Effect sizes {#sec-scale} The five results comprise a $\chi^2$ test of a table, a two-proportion test, two z statistics from logistic regressions and an omnibus test, computed on 362 to 665 emails. The robustness study chose to "transform the reported point estimates into a standard effect-size measure", noting that "these transformations have limitations and their calculation relies on assumptions that may not hold in all considered analysis settings" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136], and each statistic was converted into a correlation and then into Cohen's d. For a z statistic, the robustness study uses in its code the number of emails N in place of degrees of freedom, $r = \tanh(|z| / \sqrt{N - 3})$ with the sign of z, while a $\chi^2$ on one degree of freedom is read as the square of a z and therefore has no sign. @tbl-scale presents the resulting correlations beside the gaps in percentage points. ::: {#tbl-scale .cell tbl-cap='The published result and the five reanalyses, with the gap in percentage points (the published change in predicted probability for the OAs, the course refit for the analysts) and the correlation by the rule of the robustness study, signs as recorded. Sources: `data/reference_marks.csv`, `data/analysts5.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Result Gap (points) Recorded statistic Emails in the conversion r recorded
OAs 2017 −20.0 z = 3.73 549 0.158
8PTRZ −17.3 χ2 = 14.265 558 0.159
UYV3F −20.0 z = −3.771 362 −0.196
EWFMI −19.4 z = 3.645 549 0.155
25N5D −13.2 χ2 = 13.683 665 0.143
P9W8Y −20.0 none recorded 558 –
``` ::: ::: The same gap in percentage points can yield different correlations. UYV3F and the original authors both report a gap of twenty points, yet the two results convert to correlations of 0.196 and 0.158, because one z comes from a model without covariates on 362 replies and the other from a model with covariates and all three groups on 549. The 13.2-point gap of 25N5D converts to almost as large a correlation as the 17.3-point gap of 8PTRZ, since a correlation depends on the shares in each group and on the sizes of the groups as well as on the gap. The signs follow the statistics as typed by the analysts, with the result that the correlation of UYV3F is negative, although all five found the gap in the direction of the claim. For its effect sizes, however, the robustness study took the direction from the box ticked by each analyst, and these effect sizes therefore "are negative only when they indicate an opposite effect compared with the original study" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods]. The course expresses every result on the scale of the claim, the difference in the share of greetings in percentage points. A linear model of the 0/1 outcome yields this difference as its coefficient, and a logistic regression as an average marginal effect, that is, the change in the predicted probability of a greeting from a white to a Hispanic name, averaged over the analysed emails. @fig-marks places the six results on that scale, beside the range of the 64 specifications fitted by the course. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The published result and the five reanalyses in percentage points, against the range of the specifications on the curve of the claim (shaded). Negative values mean that Hispanic names were greeted by name less often. Sources: `data/reference_marks.csv`, `data/spec_curve.csv`.](background_files/figure-html/fig-marks-1.png){#fig-marks fig-alt='Dot chart of six results between about −20 and −13 points, with a shaded band from −20.0 to −12.1 for the curve of the claim. 25N5D lies near −13, 8PTRZ near −17, the others near −20.' width=672} ::: ::: ## 5. The replication {#sec-replication} ### 5.1 The design and the result {#sec-score-replication} The replication ([osf.io/2ug8x](https://osf.io/2ug8x/)) was a preregistered experiment of the same kind. It emailed 3,050 public housing authorities listed by HUD, not only those matched to a core city, with block randomisation within each state ensuring that every state received equal numbers of Hispanic and white names. The names were also new – Joe Garcia and Michael Hernandez against John Ryan and Nicholas Smith – and had been chosen from pre-tested names that vary perceived ethnicity while perceived class and migrant status remain similar. All four names are male, and none is meant to indicate a Black sender. The preregistration dropped the female names because, in its reading, the original study found no difference by the sex of the name, and the Black names because the claim does not concern Black names, thereby leaving more emails for each name. Replies were awaited for a week, each being coded as friendly if it used the first or the last name of the sender. The authorities sent 1,811 replies in all, and to match Table 1 the replication team retained the authorities in localities matched with census data, 2,337 emails and 1,243 replies, fitting a logistic regression with the demographic covariates used in the paper, taken from the 2018 American Community Survey, and without the Hard Email indicator. On a random draw of 738 replies, the size set by the power analysis, the coefficient of the Hispanic names was 0.098 with a standard error of 0.149 (z = 0.66, p = 0.511), and on all 1,243 replies z = 0.44 (p = 0.657), while covariates entered in thirds gave the same picture. The preregistered linear probability model without covariates, fitted on 1,000 random draws of 738 from the 1,484 replies of all authorities, found no significant difference "approximately 93 percent of the time", and SCORE judged the claim not replicated. Since a logit coefficient moves a probability by at most a quarter of its value, the slope of the logistic curve at a probability of one half, the coefficient of 0.098 corresponds to a gap of at most 2.45 points in favour of the Hispanic names. ### 5.2 On the scale of the course {#replication-scale} The replication team also published its de-identified data on the OSF ([osf.io/xseqg](https://osf.io/xseqg/)), one row for each of its 2,717 emails, with the alias, the reply and its greeting coded in the same way as in the file deposited by the original authors. From these data the course computed the same comparison as its reference specification, the difference in the share of named greetings between Hispanic and white names, with HC2 errors. Among all 1,484 replies, 52.4% of the replies to Hispanic aliases and 52.4% of the replies to white aliases opened with the name of the sender, a gap of +0.0 points (p = 0.999). Counted over all emails, with a non-reply counting as no greeting, the gap is −1.6 points (p = 0.370), and among the authorities below the county level, retained by the replication to match the paper, the gap is +0.7 points among the replies and −1.0 among all emails. The mark SCORE 2020 on the [curve of the claim](curve.qmd) represents the first of these gaps. As the licence under which the file was published is not stated, the course links to the file rather than copying it. ### 5.3 Power {#power} Power is the probability that a study detects a gap of a given size at the 5% level. @fig-power plots the power of the comparison made in the paper, with about 181 replies a group, against that of the 738 replies in the replication, split equally between the two groups, for gaps from 2 to 25 points. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The power of a two-sided test at the 5% level to detect a gap in greetings by name, below a share of 61% for the white names, for the comparison among the replies of the original study and for the 738 replies of the replication. The dotted lines mark a gap of 10 points, the near end of the published confidence interval, and of 20 points, the published estimate. Source: `data/display_power.csv`.](background_files/figure-html/fig-power-1.png){#fig-power fig-alt='Two rising power curves. The replication curve lies above the original one at every gap; at 10 points the original design has a power of about 0.48 and the replication about 0.78, and at 20 points both are close to 1.' width=720} ::: ::: The replication was sized in its preregistration so that its first round would have a power of 90% to detect three quarters of the original effect. The original design also sets a lower limit to any estimate that it can report as significant, since, with a standard error of 5.16 points for the reference comparison, a gap has to exceed 10.2 points before it clears the 5% threshold, which means that if the true gap were small, the significant estimates of a study of this size would overstate it. ### 5.4 Reading the replication {#sec-reading} Within the original data the claim appears difficult to dislodge, since reshuffling the names at random among the replies to Hispanic and white names yields gaps between −10.0 and 9.9 points in 95% of 4,999 reshuffles, far from the observed −20.0, and all 64 specifications on the curve of the claim are negative and significant, ranging from −20.0 to −12.1 points. The replication, however, shows that the same contrast, asked of a wider set of authorities in another year and with other names, gave a gap close to zero, although it does not show which of the differences between the two studies is responsible. One candidate is the names themselves, since names meant to indicate the same group are not read in the same way. @Gaddis2017HowBlackAre found that the names used in audits to indicate Black applicants are perceived as Black with varying frequency, and that names given more often by highly educated mothers are perceived as Black less often, with the implication that the findings of an audit may depend on which names represent a group. As the original authors could not match the ages implied by the Hispanic names, Santiago and Gabriela may have suggested younger senders as well as a Hispanic background, whereas the names used in the replication were chosen to hold class and migrant status constant. Chance offers a second possible explanation, given that the published interval runs from −30.5 to −10.0 points and that a study of this size detects a twenty-point gap almost always but a smaller one far less reliably. At a white rate of 61%, about 181 replies a group yield a power of 0.97 for a gap of 20 points, 0.70 for 13 and 0.48 for 10, against 0.78 for 10 points with the 369 replies a group of the replication, and a significant estimate from a study with modest power for realistic effects tends to overstate the size of such effects. Time and place form a third candidate, as the replication emailed the authorities on the HUD list six years later, and a change in who answers such emails, or how, could move the result without either study being wrong. It is around this contrast that the course is built. On one set of data the claim appears to survive every defensible analysis that the course can fit, with only its size varying, yet the analysts disagreed on whether this was evidence for the claim, and on new data nothing was found, which is why the course treats robustness to analytic choices on one sample as a property distinct from replicability. ## 6. The data you will use {#sec-data} The original authors published their data and code on the Harvard Dataverse ([doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU)) under a CC0 licence, which places the data and code in the public domain and thus allows the course to redistribute the file and everything derived from it. The public file, however, is blinded, its ReadMe explaining that census codes and continuous community values would identify the authorities, and that "Whether or not a housing official responded, particularly to an ostensible minority applicant, is very sensitive and potentially harmful information." Population, percent white, Black and Hispanic, the poverty rate and the HUD assessment score are therefore given only as thirds of the distribution of each variable (lower, middle and top). While the experimental comparisons can be reproduced exactly, the models with covariates can be reproduced only approximately, and refitted on the thirds, the model of Table 1 yields z = −3.47 and a gap of −18.4 points, against z = −3.73, the published coefficient divided by its standard error, and the published −20.0 points. No part of the course attempts to recover the continuous values withheld from the public file by this blinding. ::: {#tbl-counts .cell tbl-cap='The emails in the public file. Source: `data/housing_emails.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Emails Count
In the public file (the paper reports 1,017) 1,014
Bounced, with no reply status 23
Delivered 991
Replied 563
Replied, without a greeting code 5
Replied, with a greeting code 558
Sent to authorities without community thirds 14
Of these, replied 9
Sent to authorities without a HUD assessment third 344
``` ::: ::: The 23 bounced emails never reached an official, and the 5 uncoded replies are replies whose greeting nobody coded, the treatment of each of the two groups being one of the decisions on the [specification menu](menu.qmd). `housing_original.csv` is the public file with the column names used by the original authors, on which the reproduction of Task 3 is carried out ([codebook](data/housing_original_codebook.md)), while `housing_emails.csv` is the course file, with readable names and derived columns, on which every other exercise is based ([codebook](data/housing_emails_codebook.md)). The de-identified data of the replication, published by its team on the OSF ([osf.io/xseqg](https://osf.io/xseqg/)) without a stated licence, are in `housing_replication.csv`, in the columns of the course file, on which Task 6 fits each declared specification again ([codebook](data/housing_replication_codebook.md)).
